chunks: Designing a PCB for manufacturing. The question: How can you design a PCB for manufacturing?
Designing a PCB for manufacturing means drawing a board that the factories can build reliably and cheaply.
Each factory has limits: how thin a copper line it can etch (eat away with chemicals), how small a hole it can drill, how precisely it can place parts.
A good design stays comfortably inside those limits instead of pushing to the edge, so more boards come out good.
Think of writing a recipe for a kitchen you do not own. If the recipe needs a special oven setting that the kitchen can barely reach, many dishes will fail.
If you write for the standard equipment, with a little margin, almost every dish works. A board design is the recipe.
The factory's published capability sheet tells you what the kitchen can do, and the real limits differ between factories.
DFM rules come from each box.
Fab rules limit what the bare board can be; assembly rules limit pad shapes, spacing and thermal balance; test rules need pads at layout time; rework needs room.
Trace/space: the width of a copper line and the gap between lines, often written like 5/5 mil. A mil is a thousandth of an inch.
Annular ring: the ring of copper around a drilled hole, which must survive small drilling errors. Land pattern: the shape and size of the pads where a part is soldered.
Fiducials: alignment dots for machine cameras. Panelization: arranging boards in a frame for building.
DRC: design rule check, the software that tests your layout against the factory's limits.
Say your fab (board factory) can routinely make 4/4 mil traces and gaps. You could draw 4/4, but any small error then causes a defect, and the fab may charge extra.
Drawing 5/5 gives margin at almost no cost. Likewise you keep the ring around each hole at 0. 1 mm or more, so a slightly off-center drill still leaves copper all around.
That is the whole idea.
"I design to the factory's real capability with margin.
For the fab: comfortable trace/space, annular ring and drill aspect ratio, copper pulled back from the edge, and mask dams between fine-pitch pads.
For assembly: proper land patterns, courtyards, fiducials, consistent orientation, thermally balanced small passives, and filled via-in-pad only.
I think about the panel and test access up front, then run DRC with the fab's rules, a DFM review, and a pilot build before volume."
